# Introducing Moderation Dashboard: a streamlined interface for content moderation

Today, we’re announcing the [Moderation Dashboard](https://hivemoderation.com/dashboard) , a no-code interface for your Trust & Safety team to design and execute custom-built moderation workflows on top of Hive’s best-in-class AI models.
Moderation Dashboard enables you to set up custom rules according to your particular content policies in order to automatically take action on problematic content using Hive model results.

You can easily define sets of classification conditions and specify which of your actions – such as removing a post or banning a user – to take in response, all from within the Moderation Dashboard UI.

To do this, Moderation Dashboard administrators can set custom score ranges that trigger human review for both visual and text moderation. Content scoring in these ranges will be automatically diverted to the Review Feed for human confirmation.

When your human review rules trigger, Moderation Dashboard will route the post to the Review Feed of one of your moderators, where they can quickly visualize the post and see Hive model predictions to inform a final decision.
For each post, your moderators can select from the moderation actions you’ve set up to implement your content policy.

content.executive_summary: The term 'Needs AI Review' page describes a general concept for a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) workflow rather than a feature on a specific, universally identifiable platform. Extensive research indicates this is a functional description for a queue where AI-generated outputs requiring human oversight are sent. This report provides a comprehensive, platform-agnostic guide on how to manage and 'update' such a review system. It is based on authoritative industry best practices for HITL operations, moderation dashboards, and AI review UIs, offering a complete checklist of actionable steps covering queue design, routing rules, reviewer workflows, analytics, quality control, and feedback mechanisms to improve the overall AI system.
content.platform_identification_summary: Extensive research did not identify a specific, universally available software platform that has a dashboard page literally named 'Needs AI Review'. The provided information indicates that this terminology is a functional descriptor for a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) review queue. This feature is common in many AI and content moderation platforms, but it is not a standardized product name. For example, platforms like The Hive AI refer to it as a 'Review Feed' within their 'Moderation Dashboard,' and services like HITL.sh provide tools to build such workflows. The term 'Needs AI Review' effectively describes the purpose of the page—to hold items flagged by an AI system for human inspection—rather than being the official name of a feature on a single, specific platform.
content.conceptual_overview_of_ai_review_queues: A 'Needs AI Review' page is the user interface for a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) review queue. It functions as a critical quality control and safety mechanism for production AI systems. Its primary purpose is to intercept and route a specific subset of AI-generated outputs to human reviewers for manual inspection before they are finalized, published, or sent to end-users. This process ensures the reliability, accuracy, and safety of the AI's output. Items are typically sent to this review queue based on a set of explicit rules, such as the AI model's low confidence score for a given prediction ('confidence gating'), failure to pass automated checks ('validator failures'), flagging for sensitive or regulated content ('policy flags'), or other anomaly triggers. By having humans review these borderline or high-risk cases, organizations can prevent errors, catch policy violations, and ultimately build trust in their AI systems, all while collecting valuable data to train and improve the AI model itself.

routing_triggers_for_review.description: This rule automatically routes AI-generated outputs to a human review queue when the model's confidence score falls within a predefined uncertain range. Content with high confidence is auto-approved, while content with low confidence might be auto-rejected or escalated. This ensures human oversight is focused on borderline cases where the AI is least certain, balancing quality control with efficiency.
routing_triggers_for_review.example: An AI content generation system is configured with tiered confidence thresholds. Any output with a confidence score of 0.9 or higher is automatically approved. Outputs with scores between 0.6 and 0.89 are sent to the 'Needs AI review' queue for human verification. Outputs scoring below 0.6 are automatically rejected and flagged for analysis.

queue_design_and_management_strategies.description: This strategy utilizes a single, centralized queue for all items requiring human review. To manage workflow and ensure timely responses for critical items, each item is assigned a priority level (e.g., P0, P1, P2). Reviewers can then sort or filter the queue to address high-priority items first, ensuring that Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for the most sensitive or urgent tasks are met.
queue_design_and_management_strategies.common_use_case: This design is typically implemented as a starting point for human-in-the-loop systems, especially when the volume of reviews is manageable and the required expertise is relatively uniform across tasks. It is effective for organizations that need to balance operational simplicity with the ability to respond quickly to high-risk or time-sensitive content, such as user complaints or potential safety violations.

content.review_workflow_and_available_actions:
The core review workflow is a human-in-the-loop (HITL) process designed to ensure the quality and reliability of AI outputs. Items are routed to the 'Needs AI review' queue based on a set of explicit rules, including confidence score gating (items below a certain confidence threshold), validator failures (e.g., schema or citation errors), policy flags (sensitive categories, safety classifiers), and other escalation triggers like user complaints or novelty signals (new user intents or locales).

Once an item is in the queue, it moves through several states: 'New' → 'In review' → 'Approved' / 'Edited' / 'Rejected'. There are also states for items that require further attention, such as 'Escalated' (sent to a specialist), 'Needs clarification' (blocked pending more information), and 'Expired' (if an SLA is breached). 

A reviewer takes an item from the queue and performs one of several available actions:
- **Approve:** If the AI output is correct and meets all guidelines, it is approved.
- **Edit:** If the output is mostly correct but requires changes for correctness, completeness, tone, or format, the reviewer edits it before approval.
- **Reject:** If the output is incorrect, unsafe, or otherwise unusable, it is rejected.
- **Escalate:** If an item is particularly sensitive, high-risk, or requires a policy decision that the reviewer is not authorized to make, it is escalated to a specialist or Subject Matter Expert (SME).
- **Request Clarification:** If the reviewer lacks the necessary context to make a decision, they can flag the item as blocked.

To ensure high throughput and generate structured feedback, reviewers use a rubric and a set of structured decision codes (e.g., INCORRECT, INCOMPLETE, UNSAFE, FORMAT_FAIL) to categorize the reason for their action, often supplemented by short notes rather than long free-text explanations.

reviewer_roles_and_responsibilities.primary_responsibilities: A Quality Reviewer is responsible for conducting in-depth evaluations of AI-generated outputs that have been flagged in the review queue. Their main tasks include carefully editing content to ensure it meets standards for correctness, completeness, tone, and formatting. They must also verify that the output complies with all relevant policies. A key part of their duty is to apply structured decision codes (e.g., INCORRECT, INCOMPLETE) to accurately categorize the outcome of each review, providing valuable data for system improvement.
reviewer_roles_and_responsibilities.decision_authority: The Quality Reviewer is empowered to make the final decision on most items in their queue, with the authority to approve, edit, or reject the AI output. However, their authority is bounded; they are expected to escalate cases that fall outside their expertise or established policy. This includes escalating sensitive or high-risk content to designated Specialists (SMEs) and escalating issues that would require inventing new policy to a Queue Lead or policy team.

content.dashboard_ui_best_practices:
An effective review dashboard UI should be designed to maximize reviewer efficiency, clarity, and the quality of feedback. A core principle is to surface all necessary context inline to minimize context switching; this includes creating a dedicated context panel that shows user inputs, intermediate LLM traces, model predictions, and any related reference materials. The UI must feature a clear and accessible action bar with primary actions like 'Approve', 'Edit', 'Reject', and 'Escalate', paired with a structured decision-code selector and a field for short notes.

To boost throughput, the dashboard should incorporate several efficiency-oriented features. These include bulk actions for triaging homogeneous items, keyboard shortcuts for common actions, and templates for standard edits. The interface should clearly communicate urgency and status through visual cues like priority badges (P0/P1/P2) and SLA countdown timers. It's also crucial to show clear ownership and assignment status for each item.

Beyond simple review, the UI should empower reviewers to improve the AI system. This means providing tools to identify and tag specific failure modes, suggest improvements, and even directly tag cases to be added to regression test datasets or file bug reports with pre-filled trace details. Finally, the dashboard should be customizable on a per-user basis, allowing reviewers to configure their widget layout, set default filters and views, and manage notification preferences to create their optimal work environment.

performance_metrics_and_slas.description: This metric measures the total time elapsed from when an item is first routed into the 'Needs AI review' queue until a human reviewer makes a final decision on it (e.g., Approved, Edited, Rejected, or Escalated). It is a critical indicator of the efficiency and responsiveness of the human review process, directly impacting how quickly AI-generated content is finalized and whether backlogs are growing or shrinking.

quality_assurance_and_auditing_methods.description: This method involves having a subset of items that have already been reviewed by one person be independently reviewed by a second person (often a more senior reviewer or QA specialist). The decisions and edits from both reviewers are then compared to identify discrepancies.
quality_assurance_and_auditing_methods.goal: The primary objective is to measure and improve the consistency and accuracy of human reviewers. By analyzing agreement rates, the system can identify ambiguities in the review rubric, pinpoint training needs for individual reviewers, and ensure that quality standards are being met consistently across the team.

content.feedback_loop_implementation: The outcomes of the review process are systematically captured and fed back to improve the AI system. This is achieved by creating a data pipeline that collects structured signals from the 'Needs AI review' page. Key captured data includes the final decision codes (e.g., INCORRECT, UNSAFE, FORMAT_FAIL), any human-made edits to the AI's output, the specific triggers that sent the item to review (e.g., low confidence score, policy flag), and other outcome signals. This curated data is then used in several ways: it is fed into evaluation datasets to better measure model performance on challenging cases; it informs updates to prompts, automated validators, and routing rule thresholds; and the impact of these changes is measured against downstream KPIs. The system also provides in-flow paths for reviewers to directly suggest improvements or trigger updates to knowledge bases or prompts, creating a continuous improvement cycle.

cost_management_levers.description: This involves refining the rules that send items to the 'Needs AI Review' queue. By implementing better validators, improving AI prompts to generate more accurate outputs, and fine-tuning routing thresholds, fewer items will be flagged for manual review. This directly reduces the workload on the review team.
